difficultyReason: The argument makes two moves: it cites an opposing view and then attacks it by invoking a general principle. Students must track both moves to identify the correct answer; traps describe only one move or mislabel the technique.
stimulus: Historian: Some scholars argue that the decline of the Roman Empire was primarily caused by military overextension. But this explanation cannot be correct. Any empire whose administrative capacity grows proportionally with its territorial expansion will not collapse for military reasons alone. Rome's administrative infrastructure actually kept pace with its expansion for most of the imperial period — it was internal political fragmentation, not overextension, that eroded Roman cohesion.

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing statistical evidence to establish that military overextension was less severe than previous scholars believed

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting a proposed explanation by showing that the conditions required for that explanation to apply were not present

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between Rome's administrative system and those of other empires that did not collapse

choices.label: D
choices.text: establishing a general causal principle and then offering Rome as the primary evidence for that principle

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that military overextension played a role in Rome's decline while arguing that internal factors were more decisive

explanations.correct: The historian first states a general principle (an empire whose administration grows proportionally with expansion won't collapse from military overextension alone), then shows that Rome's administration did keep pace — meaning the condition required for the military-overextension explanation does not hold. This is precisely what B describes: rejecting an explanation by showing its required conditions were absent.
explanations.A: No statistical evidence is cited; the historian makes a structural argument about administrative capacity. This answer imports content not in the stimulus.
explanations.C: No analogy to other empires appears; the argument stays focused on Rome and an abstract principle. This is an 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.D: The principle is not derived from Rome — it is stated independently and then applied to Rome. D reverses the logical direction.
explanations.E: The historian does not concede that military overextension played any role; the argument rejects that explanation outright. 'Conceding' is an extreme-mischaracterization trap.

difficultyReason: The argument sets up a symmetry between two cases and draws an inference from the one where evidence is available to the one where it is not. Traps either mislabel the move as causal or describe a generalization rather than an analogy.
stimulus: Physician: We have extensive outcome data on patients who received the newer minimally invasive procedure for gallstone removal, and those outcomes were no better than outcomes for the traditional open surgery. We have no comparable outcome data yet for the newer procedure as applied to elderly patients with multiple comorbidities, because that population was excluded from early trials. Given the similarity of the underlying physiology, however, the newer procedure likely offers no advantage over open surgery for elderly patients either.
questionStem: The physician's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers that two medical procedures are equally risky by showing that they share the same physiological mechanism

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses outcome data from a general population to derive a statistical generalization applicable to all surgical patients

choices.label: C
choices.text: uses a case in which direct evidence is available to draw a conclusion about an analogous case in which direct evidence is unavailable

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejects a proposed treatment protocol by showing that it contradicts well-established physiological principles

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases a prediction about future clinical outcomes on a controlled experimental study involving elderly patients

explanations.correct: The physician has direct outcome data for general patients (evidence available) and no direct data for elderly patients (evidence unavailable). The analogy between the two groups — grounded in similar physiology — bridges the gap. This is exactly what C describes, mirroring the structure of the authentic LSAC anchor question.
explanations.A: The argument is about comparative effectiveness, not comparative risk. 'Equally risky' misrepresents the conclusion, and 'same physiological mechanism' overstates the claim. This is a content-echoing trap.
explanations.B: The argument does not derive a statistical generalization applicable to all surgical patients — it draws a specific conclusion about elderly patients. 'All surgical patients' is an over-generalization trap.
explanations.D: No treatment protocol is rejected, and no contradiction with physiological principles is alleged. This describes a different type of argument entirely.
explanations.E: There is no controlled experimental study involving elderly patients — that is precisely what is lacking. This answer inverts the evidential situation described in the stimulus.

difficultyReason: The argument invokes a definition to settle an apparently empirical dispute. Students must recognize that the key move is definitional rather than evidential, causal, or analogical — traps dress up each of those alternatives plausibly.
stimulus: Economist: Critics of free-trade agreements claim that such agreements harm workers by suppressing wages. But wages in industries exposed to import competition have, in several well-documented cases, actually risen in the years following trade liberalization. This shows that free-trade agreements do not harm workers in the relevant sense — because economic harm to workers, properly understood, means a reduction in real compensation, and no such reduction has occurred in these cases.
questionStem: The economist's argument derives its conclusion by

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to a definition of economic harm to show that the critics' evidence does not establish the critics' conclusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing a counterexample to the universal claim that free-trade agreements always benefit workers

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that the causal mechanism proposed by critics cannot produce the effect they allege

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between wage trends in trade-exposed industries and wage trends in protected industries

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring from a sample of industries that free-trade agreements universally raise wages across all economic sectors

explanations.correct: The economist's key move is definitional: economic harm to workers means reduction in real compensation. Having established that definition, the economist notes wages rose, so no harm occurred in the defined sense. The critics' conclusion is undercut not by disputing their evidence but by showing the evidence doesn't satisfy the definition of 'harm.'
explanations.B: The argument does not offer a counterexample to a claim that free trade always benefits workers — it defends free trade against critics. The direction of the argument is reversed. This is an 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.C: No causal mechanism is examined or refuted; the economist does not engage with why wages rose, only with whether the outcome counts as harm. This describes a causal-rebuttal argument not present here.
explanations.D: No analogy to protected industries appears in the stimulus. This introduces content absent from the argument.
explanations.E: The economist draws a specific conclusion about cases of trade liberalization, not a universal generalization about all sectors. 'Universally raises wages' is an extreme-verb trap.

difficultyReason: The argument eliminates alternatives to arrive at its conclusion, a technique students often confuse with simple generalization or counterexample citation. Two traps each partially describe part of the argument without capturing the elimination structure.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: The sharp decline in the local honeybee population over the past decade must be attributable to pesticide exposure. It cannot be explained by habitat loss, because the wildflower meadows in the region have actually expanded during this period. It cannot be explained by disease, because pathogen surveys have found no novel pathogens in the hives. With the other leading explanations ruled out, pesticide exposure is the only remaining candidate.
questionStem: The environmental scientist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifying a correlation between pesticide use and bee population decline and inferring that the correlation reflects a causal relationship

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general ecological principle to predict the consequences of pesticide exposure for pollinator populations

choices.label: C
choices.text: eliminating alternative explanations for a phenomenon in order to conclude that a particular explanation must be correct

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing experimental evidence that directly links pesticide compounds to the observed decline in bee populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that habitat loss and disease are contributing factors while arguing that pesticide exposure is the dominant cause

explanations.correct: The scientist does not present positive evidence for pesticide exposure; instead, the argument proceeds by ruling out habitat loss and disease and concluding that pesticide exposure must therefore be the explanation. This is argument by elimination — exactly what C describes.
explanations.A: No correlation between pesticide use and bee decline is stated in the stimulus; the argument never establishes that pesticide exposure actually occurred at elevated levels. This is a content-importing trap.
explanations.B: No general ecological principle is cited or applied. The argument is particular and eliminative, not principle-driven.
explanations.D: No experimental evidence is mentioned; the stimulus explicitly relies on ruling out alternatives rather than on direct positive evidence. 'Directly links' is an extreme-verb trap.
explanations.E: The scientist does not concede that habitat loss and disease are contributing factors — the argument explicitly rules them out. This is a mischaracterization trap that reverses the logical force of the premises.

difficultyReason: The argument applies an abstract principle to a specific case, but the principle is embedded in a counterargument structure, making it easy to misidentify the main move. Traps either describe the counterargument alone or mislabel the move as an analogy.
stimulus: Ethicist: Some argue that it is always permissible to break a promise when doing so would produce better overall consequences. But a legal contract that could be voided whenever a party believed doing so would yield better outcomes would provide no meaningful security to anyone who relied on it. The same is true of personal promises: a norm permitting promise-breaking whenever consequences favor it would undermine the very practice of promising, since no rational person would rely on a promise made under such a norm.
questionStem: Which one of the following describes a technique of reasoning used in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between legal contracts and personal promises to argue that the same standard of permissibility should govern both

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing an authority on contract law to establish that promise-breaking is impermissible under existing legal standards

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting a normative claim by showing that universally applying it would produce a result incompatible with the purpose the norm is meant to serve

choices.label: D
choices.text: offering a series of historical counterexamples to demonstrate that consequentialist ethics has never successfully guided promise-keeping behavior

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that consequences are morally relevant while arguing that they are not the only consideration in evaluating promises

explanations.correct: The ethicist's central move is a reductio-style rejection: if the norm 'break promises whenever consequences favor it' were universally applied, it would destroy the practice of promising itself — a result incompatible with the norm's own purpose. The legal-contract case is an illustration of this self-defeating quality, not the main technique. C captures the full move accurately.
explanations.A: The analogy to legal contracts is an illustrative device, not the main technique. The argument's conclusion is about promising in general, not about aligning legal and personal standards. Selecting A would be a 'partially true' trap — the analogy is present but is not the primary reasoning technique.
explanations.B: No legal authority is cited; the legal-contract example is used analogically, not as an appeal to authority. This describes a move the argument does not make.
explanations.D: No historical counterexamples are offered; the argument is abstract and hypothetical, not historical. This is an 'accurate description of a different argument' trap.
explanations.E: The ethicist does not concede that consequences are morally relevant — the argument attacks the consequentialist norm directly. 'Conceding' misrepresents the rhetorical posture of the argument.
